summaries.example: Imagine you see a real zebra in a zoo enclosure. You know, or seem to know, that it is a zebra. A zebra is not a cleverly disguised mule, so you may reason that it is not a mule. Some philosophers say this new conclusion is also knowledge. Others say that seeing a zebra gives you a good reason about the zebra, but does not by itself rule out every strange possibility.
summaries.summary: Epistemic closure is the idea that knowledge can extend through logic. If you know one fact and understand that another fact follows from it, it seems reasonable to think you can know the second fact too. For example, if you know an animal is a zebra, and you know that a zebra is not a mule, you might think you know it is not a mule. But some philosophers disagree. They argue that knowing the first fact may not mean that you can rule out every unusual possibility connected with the second fact. The entry examines several ways to understand knowledge, including tracking, relevant alternatives, safe indication, and reliabilism. It also considers skeptical challenges, such as whether ordinary knowledge can rule out being completely deceived. The discussion shows why a simple rule about knowledge must be qualified and why philosophers continue to debate whether knowledge and justified belief spread through logical consequences.
key_ideas: The closure principle says that knowledge can spread from a known fact to facts that logically follow from it.
The principle needs careful wording. A person may fail to notice the connection, reason badly, or stop believing the first fact.
Some philosophers reject closure because a person may know an ordinary fact without knowing that unusual alternatives are false.
Other philosophers defend closure by saying that good evidence for one fact can also support facts that follow from it.
Similar questions arise about justified belief, but knowing and having a justified belief are not exactly the same.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us understand how reasoning changes what we know. It also shows why a conclusion can feel obvious while still raising questions about evidence, mistakes, and unusual possibilities. These questions matter whenever we decide whether a reason really supports a conclusion.

important_terms.definition: Knowing one fact can sometimes put you in a position to know another fact that follows from it.
A statement or idea that must be true if another statement is true.
A belief that we have good reasons to hold, even though it might still be wrong.
A possible situation that would make something you believe false, such as being fooled by a very clever trick.

questions_to_think_about: If you know there are three apples in a bowl, do you also know there is at least one apple?
Does seeing a zebra give you enough reason to know it is not a disguised mule?
Can a person have a good reason for a belief without actually knowing that the belief is true?

summaries.example: Suppose you are looking at an ordinary zoo enclosure. You know that the animal is a zebra because of your visual experience. From the proposition that it is a zebra, you infer that it is not a cleverly disguised mule. A tracking theorist may say that you know the first proposition but not the second: if the animal were a mule, you might still have the same zebra-like experience and make the same inference. A defender of safe indication may respond that, in these circumstances, the evidence would not occur unless the relevant claim were true, so closure can be preserved.
summaries.summary: Epistemic closure concerns whether knowledge is preserved under entailment. The intuitive idea is that if a person knows p and recognizes that p entails q, then the person should be able to know q. The entry argues that the unrestricted version is inadequate because people can fail to notice an implication, reason incompetently, or abandon their original belief. A more carefully qualified principle is therefore the main target of debate. Tracking accounts of knowledge require that a person would not believe p in nearby cases where p is false. The zebra example suggests that a person may track the ordinary claim while failing to track a consequence that rules out a strange alternative. Relevant-alternatives accounts likewise may reject closure if the negation of a claim must be ruled out even when it is not a relevant alternative to an implication of that claim. In contrast, safe-indication accounts and some versions of reliabilism support closure, though safety may not by itself guarantee knowledge. The entry also considers arguments from limiting propositions, lottery propositions, skeptical hypotheses, and the nonclosure of particular knowledge-producing methods. Finally, it separates closure of knowledge from closure of justified belief, noting that probability-based justification can fail to survive repeated conjunction.
key_ideas: The strongest informal version of closure is too simple: knowing p does not guarantee knowing q if one fails to see the entailment, reasons incorrectly, or withdraws belief in p.
A qualified principle says that if someone knows p, believes q because they recognize that p entails q, and retains the relevant knowledge, then the person knows q.
Tracking theories produce counterexamples: the evidence may support knowledge of an ordinary claim while remaining compatible with a nearby situation in which its consequence is false.

Safe-indication theories can support closure because if a reason safely indicates p, and p entails q, that reason can safely indicate q as well; however, safety alone may not be sufficient for knowledge.
Relevant-alternatives theories do not have one inevitable result. Some versions reject closure, while others treat remote alternatives as irrelevant and preserve it.

The entry distinguishes knowledge closure from closure of justified belief. Combining many individually justified lottery beliefs can produce an unjustified conjunction, threatening some forms of justification closure.
summaries.why_it_matters: Closure sits at the intersection of logic, evidence, skepticism, and everyday reasoning. It asks whether a good argument from something known can itself produce knowledge, rather than merely a plausible belief. The competing answers reveal that the result depends not only on logical implication but also on how knowledge, evidence, reliability, and context are understood.

important_terms.definition: The thesis that, under suitable conditions, knowing p and recognizing that p entails q can place a person in a position to know q.
A relation in which q must be true whenever p is true; q is then a logical consequence of p.
An account of knowledge requiring that, in nearby situations where p is false, the subject would not continue believing p, often through the same method.
A view that knowledge requires ruling out alternatives that matter in the subject's circumstances, but not every imaginable alternative.
A condition according to which a reason for believing p would not hold unless p were true, or would reliably indicate p in nearby cases.
An approach linking knowledge to belief formed or maintained by a reliable method; different accounts define reliability differently.
The position that standards for attributing knowledge can vary with the context of the person making the judgment.
A proposition that seems difficult to know, such as a lottery claim or the denial of a skeptical hypothesis, despite following from ordinary claims.

questions_to_think_about: Should knowing an ordinary proposition automatically include knowing that every skeptical hypothesis inconsistent with it is false?
Does the zebra example show that closure fails, or does it reveal a weakness in the tracking account?
Can a reason be safe enough to support knowledge without being sufficient on its own?
Why might each ticket's likely loss be justified while the claim that every ticket will lose is not?
Does contextualism explain skepticism more successfully by changing standards rather than rejecting closure?

summaries.example: You are at a zoo and see an animal in a cage labeled “zebra.” It really is a zebra, and your view is normal. You seem to know that it is a zebra. You then notice that being a zebra rules out being a disguised mule. Does your knowledge automatically include the fact that it is not a mule? One philosopher might say yes because the second fact follows from the first. Another might say no because your eyes could give you the same kind of zebra experience even in a strange situation involving a mule.
summaries.summary: Epistemic closure is a proposed rule about how knowledge works. In its simplest form, it says that if someone knows p, and p logically guarantees q, then that person knows q. The source explains why this rule is attractive but also why it cannot be stated without qualifications. Someone may not understand the logic, may reason badly, or may stop knowing p during the process. More importantly, some theories of knowledge say that a person must be able to rule out certain nearby ways of being wrong. On a tracking theory, a person knows p only if they would not believe p in nearby situations where p is false. This can make it possible to know that an animal is a zebra without knowing that it is not a disguised mule. Relevant-alternatives theories may reach a similar result, although other versions preserve closure by treating remote possibilities as unimportant. Safe-indication theories and some reliabilist theories defend closure in a different way: reliable evidence for p can also support consequences of p. The entry connects these debates with skepticism, lottery cases, and the question of whether justified belief spreads through logical reasoning.
key_ideas: The basic closure idea is appealing: if you know one fact and understand its logical consequence, you should be able to know the consequence.
The principle must be qualified because people can miss an implication, reason incorrectly, or lose their original knowledge while thinking through the consequence.
Tracking and some relevant-alternatives theories give cases in which an ordinary fact is known but a connected consequence is not.
Safe-indication theories and some forms of reliabilism offer ways to defend closure, although philosophers debate whether safety alone is enough.
Skepticism uses closure to argue from uncertainty about strange possibilities to uncertainty about everyday facts.
Closure for justified belief is also disputed: many likely beliefs can combine into a claim that is not itself sufficiently likely.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue helps explain why reasoning from evidence is sometimes straightforward and sometimes controversial. It also shows why philosophers disagree about skepticism: some reject the rule that knowledge spreads, while others keep the rule and change their account of evidence or context. Understanding the disagreement improves our ability to separate logic from assumptions about what knowledge requires.

important_terms.definition: The idea that knowledge can be extended to a fact that logically follows from something already known.
A logical connection in which one claim guarantees that another claim is true.
A possible explanation or situation that would make a claim false and may need to be ruled out.
An account saying that knowledge depends on whether a person would continue believing a claim in nearby situations where it is false.
An account saying that evidence is dependable when it would not occur unless the claim it supports were true.
A theory connecting knowledge with methods that usually lead to true beliefs.
A position that says what counts as knowledge can change when the conversational or intellectual situation changes.

questions_to_think_about: If one fact logically guarantees another, should knowing the first always mean knowing the second?
Is the zebra case a problem for closure itself, or only for one theory of knowledge?
What makes an unusual alternative important enough that we must rule it out?
Why might knowing be stricter than having a belief that is very likely?
How could changing the standards of a discussion affect whether someone counts as knowing?
